125:   metabolism: [
126:     { topic: 'ATP in the cell', correct: 'It is a portable energy currency that links energy-releasing and energy-requiring processes.', wrongs: ['It is the cell’s long-term fuel store.', 'It is a permanent membrane component.', 'It is an enzyme.'], why: 'ATP can transfer a phosphate group or release free energy to drive otherwise unfavorable reactions, but it is not stored long term.', analogy: 'It is like cash used for daily transactions instead of a vault of savings.' },
127:     { topic: 'ATP hydrolysis', correct: 'It usually yields ADP and inorganic phosphate while releasing free energy.', wrongs: ['It produces glucose and oxygen.', 'It yields only AMP with no phosphate.', 'It always creates DNA.'], why: 'Cleaving the terminal phosphoanhydride bond releases energy that can be coupled to work.', analogy: 'It is like breaking a spring-loaded latch to release stored force.' },
128:     { topic: 'glycolysis', correct: 'It is the pathway that breaks glucose into pyruvate in the cytosol.', wrongs: ['It is the mitochondrial pathway for fatty acid synthesis.', 'It directly makes ATP synthase.', 'It produces only glycogen.'], why: 'Glycolysis converts glucose into a smaller carbon compound and captures some energy in ATP and NADH.', analogy: 'It is like taking a large crate and unpacking it into smaller pieces while collecting some energy along the way.' },
129:     { topic: 'oxidation in metabolism', correct: 'It is the loss of electrons, often associated with the release of energy.', wrongs: ['It is the gain of electrons.', 'It is the same as adding oxygen only.', 'It always means a cell is becoming basic.'], why: 'Redox chemistry is central to nutrient breakdown and ATP generation.', analogy: 'It is like a battery losing charge as it powers a device.' },
130:     { topic: 'NAD+ in metabolism', correct: 'It accepts electrons and becomes NADH, carrying reducing power to other pathways.', wrongs: ['It stores genetic information.', 'It is a membrane lipid.', 'It destroys all ATP.'], why: 'NAD+ is a universal electron carrier that cycles between oxidized and reduced forms.', analogy: 'It is like a rechargeable battery that picks up and delivers energy packets.' },
131:     { topic: 'the citric acid cycle', correct: 'It oxidizes acetyl-CoA and produces reduced electron carriers and some ATP equivalents.', wrongs: ['It is the pathway that makes proteins from DNA.', 'It only occurs in the cytosol.', 'It is a direct glucose breakdown pathway.',], why: 'The cycle completes oxidation of fuel-derived carbons and generates high-energy electron carriers.', analogy: 'It is like a central sorting hub where fuel is squeezed to release energy.' },
132:     { topic: 'oxidative phosphorylation', correct: 'It uses the electron transport chain and ATP synthase to generate most ATP in aerobic cells.', wrongs: ['It is the pathway for DNA transcription.', 'It stores glycogen in the liver.', 'It occurs only in the cytosol.'], why: 'A proton gradient powers ATP synthase as electrons flow through the chain to oxygen.', analogy: 'It is like a water wheel driven by a pressure difference.' },
133:     { topic: 'the role of oxygen in aerobic metabolism', correct: 'It acts as the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain.', wrongs: ['It is the main substrate for glycolysis.', 'It is only used to make glucose.', 'It stores high-energy phosphate.'], why: 'Oxygen accepts electrons and protons to form water, allowing the chain to continue running.', analogy: 'It is like the final destination for a conveyor belt of electrons.' },
134:     { topic: 'the purpose of catabolism', correct: 'It breaks down nutrients to release energy and produce precursors for biosynthesis.', wrongs: ['It only builds proteins from scratch.', 'It never releases energy.', 'It stores all energy as ATP forever.'], why: 'Catabolism converts fuel molecules into usable energy and smaller building blocks.', analogy: 'It is like disassembling a structure to recover parts and power the next job.' },
135:     { topic: 'the purpose of anabolism', correct: 'It builds complex molecules from simpler precursors using energy.', wrongs: ['It only breaks down ATP.', 'It is the same as glycolysis.', 'It never needs enzyme catalysis.'], why: 'Biosynthesis requires energy to assemble molecules such as proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids.', analogy: 'It is like using energy and tools to construct a house from bricks.' },
136:     { topic: 'the significance of coupled reactions', correct: 'An unfavorable reaction can proceed when linked to a favorable one such as ATP hydrolysis.', wrongs: ['They always have the same enzyme.', 'They always release no heat.', 'They are only found in DNA replication.'], why: 'Shared intermediates and energy coupling make otherwise impossible reactions possible in cells.', analogy: 'It is like pushing a cart downhill to get it over a hill.' },
137:     { topic: 'a reducing equivalent', correct: 'It is an electron or electron pair carried by cofactors such as NADH or FADH2.', wrongs: ['It is a protein polymer.', 'It is a lipid tail.', 'It is a phosphate storage unit.'], why: 'Metabolic pathways move electrons through carriers to enable controlled energy transfer.', analogy: 'It is like moving a parcel from one station to another in a delivery system.' },
138:     { topic: 'the role of CoA in metabolism', correct: 'It carries acyl groups and helps activate them for oxidation or synthesis.', wrongs: ['It only binds DNA.', 'It breaks down proteins.', 'It is always an enzyme.'], why: 'CoA forms thioester bonds with acyl groups and allows transfer in pathways like the citric acid cycle and fatty acid metabolism.', analogy: 'It is like a labeled cart carrying a load through the factory floor.' },
139:     { topic: 'the meaning of phosphorylation potential', correct: 'It reflects the free-energy available from ATP hydrolysis under a given cellular condition.', wrongs: ['It is a simple count of phosphate groups.', 'It measures pH only.', 'It always equals zero.'], why: 'The energy available from ATP depends on substrate and product concentrations as well as reaction conditions.', analogy: 'It is like measuring how much force a spring can still release after being partially compressed.' },
140:     { topic: 'the purpose of glycogen in animals', correct: 'It stores glucose for rapid mobilization when energy demand rises.', wrongs: ['It stores ATP permanently.', 'It is a structural protein.', 'It forms the membrane barrier.'], why: 'Glycogen provides a compact short-term energy reserve in liver and muscle.', analogy: 'It is like keeping emergency fuel on hand in a supply locker.' },
141:     { topic: 'fatty acid beta oxidation', correct: 'It breaks fatty acids into acetyl-CoA units for the citric acid cycle.', wrongs: ['It is the process that builds DNA.', 'It only happens in the nucleus.', 'It produces only ATP without acetyl-CoA.'], why: 'Repeated oxidation removes two-carbon units from the fatty acid chain and yields reduced cofactors.', analogy: 'It is like chopping a long log into usable firewood pieces.' },
142:     { topic: 'the reason cells use multiple steps in metabolism', correct: 'Multiple steps allow regulation, energy capture, and controlled conversion of nutrients.', wrongs: ['Multiple steps are unnecessary and wasteful.', 'Every step must be instantaneous and direct.', 'Multiple steps always reduce ATP output.'], why: 'Pathways can control flux and recover energy gradually instead of in one explosive burst.', analogy: 'It is like moving through a series of checkpoints rather than jumping the whole course at once.' },
143:     { topic: 'the role of enzymes in metabolism', correct: 'They lower activation barriers and increase the rate of specific biochemical reactions.', wrongs: ['They change the equilibrium position of reactions.', 'They are always consumed in each reaction.', 'They carry genetic information.'], why: 'Enzymes speed up reactions without altering the basic thermodynamics of the process.', analogy: 'They are like experienced guides making a difficult path easier to traverse.' },
144:     { topic: 'the purpose of metabolic regulation', correct: 'It controls pathway flux to match cellular supply, demand, and energy status.', wrongs: ['It makes every pathway run continuously at full speed.', 'It eliminates all feedback control.', 'It is relevant only in plants.'], why: 'Cells adjust enzyme activity and substrate availability to maintain homeostasis and efficiency.', analogy: 'It is like a traffic control system that changes lights according to congestion.' },
145:     { topic: 'the importance of phosphates in metabolism', correct: 'Phosphate groups provide a way to store and transfer energy and regulate biomolecules.', wrongs: ['Phosphates are only structural and never energetic.', 'They only occur in DNA.', 'They are replaced by sulfur groups in all cells.'], why: 'High-energy phosphate bonds and phosphorylation states change reactivity and signaling.', analogy: 'They are like convenient tags and energy packets attached to molecules.' },
146:     { topic: 'the role of glucagon in carbohydrate metabolism', correct: 'It signals the liver to mobilize stored fuels and raise blood glucose when needed.', wrongs: ['It stimulates direct ATP synthesis in all cells.', 'It only acts on RNA.', 'It always lowers blood sugar.'], why: 'Hormones coordinate energy balance in response to physiological needs.', analogy: 'It is like a signal telling the warehouse to release stock when demand rises.' },
147:     { topic: 'the role of insulin', correct: 'It helps promote uptake and storage of nutrients, especially after feeding.', wrongs: ['It acts only in the nucleus with no other effects.', 'It permanently degrades all glucose.', 'It prevents metabolism from happening.'], why: 'Insulin signaling increases nutrient uptake and anabolic pathways in many tissues.', analogy: 'It is like a store manager telling the system to restock and store supplies after a delivery.' },
148:     { topic: 'the meaning of metabolic flux', correct: 'It is the rate of flow of molecules through a pathway under cellular conditions.', wrongs: ['It is the size of the organelle membrane.', 'It is the same as the number of enzymes.', 'It is only a pH measure.'], why: 'Flux depends on enzyme rates, substrate levels, and regulation of the network.', analogy: 'It is like how much traffic moves along a highway at a given time.' },
149:     { topic: 'the purpose of the pentose phosphate pathway', correct: 'It produces NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate needed for biosynthesis and antioxidant defense.', wrongs: ['It only breaks down proteins.', 'It is absent in most cells.', 'It directly makes ATP and no other product.'], why: 'The pathway supports biosynthesis and helps protect against oxidative stress by generating reducing power.', analogy: 'It is like a side workshop that makes both building materials and protective gear.' },
150:     { topic: 'the role of FAD in metabolism', correct: 'It accepts electrons as part of redox reactions and carries them to the electron transport chain.', wrongs: ['It stores permanent DNA.', 'It breaks peptide bonds.', 'It acts only as a base.'], why: 'FAD and FADH2 are electron carriers with different oxidation states used in metabolic pathways.', analogy: 'It is like a relay runner handing off energy to the next stage.' },
151:     { topic: 'the relationship between oxidation and reduction', correct: 'They are coupled: one molecule is oxidized as another is reduced.', wrongs: ['They are independent and never linked.', 'Oxidation always occurs without any electron movement.', 'Reduction means losing oxygen only.'], why: 'Electron transfer is balanced, preserving charge within the system.', analogy: 'It is like one person handing a baton to another while both keep the race moving.' },
152:     { topic: 'the reason ATP is considered high energy', correct: 'Its hydrolysis releases substantial free energy because of charge repulsion, resonance, and solvation effects.', wrongs: ['It is high energy because it contains only carbon atoms.', 'It is high energy because it is always stored in large amounts.', 'It is high energy only when surrounded by oxygen.'], why: 'The products of ATP hydrolysis are more stable than ATP itself, so the reaction releases free energy.', analogy: 'It is like a stretched spring that releases a strong push when released.' },
153:     { topic: 'the effect of allosteric regulation', correct: 'It changes enzyme activity by binding a site other than the active site.', wrongs: ['It always destroys the enzyme.', 'It binds only the DNA coding region.', 'It only affects pH.'], why: 'Allosteric regulators shift protein conformation and therefore enzyme activity.', analogy: 'It is like adjusting the steering of a car without touching the wheel directly.' },
154:     { topic: 'feedback inhibition', correct: 'It is a regulatory mechanism in which the end product of a pathway inhibits an earlier step.', wrongs: ['It always accelerates the pathway to a maximum rate.', 'It is only a pH phenomenon.', 'It creates ATP without regulation.'], why: 'This prevents excess product and helps balance supply and demand in metabolism.', analogy: 'It is like a thermostat turning down a heater when the room is already warm.' },
155:     { topic: 'the role of pyruvate', correct: 'It is the end product of glycolysis and a key branch point in metabolism.', wrongs: ['It is the final product of the citric acid cycle.', 'It is only used to build DNA.', 'It is a membrane lipid.'], why: 'Pyruvate can be converted to acetyl-CoA, lactate, or oxaloacetate depending on cell conditions.', analogy: 'It is like a junction station where travelers can take different routes.' },
156:     { topic: 'the difference between substrate-level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation', correct: 'Substrate-level phosphorylation transfers a phosphate directly from a substrate to ADP, while oxidative phosphorylation uses a proton gradient.', wrongs: ['They are identical and only differ by naming.', 'Only oxidative phosphorylation happens in the cytosol.', 'Substrate-level phosphorylation only uses oxygen.'], why: 'The mechanism and location of ATP formation differ between the two processes.', analogy: 'It is like making a purchase either by giving cash directly or by using a machine that converts a stored charge.' },
157:     { topic: 'the function of lactate fermentation', correct: 'It regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue when oxygen is limited.', wrongs: ['It produces oxygen for the electron transport chain.', 'It stores glycogen in the liver.', 'It directly creates ATP from glucose without enzymes.'], why: 'Fermentation allows glycolysis to continue under anaerobic conditions by reoxidizing NADH.', analogy: 'It is like refilling a runner’s energy cups so the race can continue.' },
158:     { topic: 'the relevance of the electron transport chain to ATP production', correct: 'It creates a proton motive force that drives ATP synthase.', wrongs: ['It breaks ATP directly to make oxygen.', 'It stores all electrons in glycogen.', 'It bypasses the need for membranes.'], why: 'Electron flow establishes a gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane.', analogy: 'It is like pumping water uphill to later turn a turbine.' },
159:     { topic: 'the fate of acetyl-CoA in metabolism', correct: 'It can enter the citric acid cycle for oxidation or be used in biosynthesis depending on cellular needs.', wrongs: ['It is always immediately excreted.', 'It can only make DNA.', 'It never participates in metabolism.'], why: 'Acetyl-CoA is a crossroads metabolite linking carbohydrate, fat, and amino acid metabolism.', analogy: 'It is like a train switching between different routes depending on the schedule.' },
160:     { topic: 'the reason cells prefer stepwise oxidation of fuels', correct: 'It captures energy in manageable amounts and allows controlled coupling to ATP synthesis.', wrongs: ['It maximizes heat release without control.', 'It is only to make carbon dioxide.', 'It eliminates redox chemistry.'], why: 'Gradual extraction of electrons prevents runaway heat and preserves energy as ATP or reducing power.', analogy: 'It is like letting water flow through multiple turbines instead of crashing in one big waterfall.' },
161:     { topic: 'the role of mitochondrial membranes in metabolism', correct: 'They compartmentalize the electron transport chain and allow generation of a proton gradient.', wrongs: ['They are only decorative and never used in metabolism.', 'They increase pH without any effect on ATP synthesis.', 'They prevent all molecules from entering the matrix.'], why: 'Membranes create the separation needed for a proton motive force.', analogy: 'They are like a dam that creates a pressure difference for generating power.' },
162:     { topic: 'the meaning of anabolic and catabolic balance', correct: 'Cells maintain a coordinated balance so energy is stored or released as needed by physiological conditions.', wrongs: ['They are always unrelated and never connected.', 'Only catabolism matters in a living cell.', 'Anabolism only occurs in plants.'], why: 'The cell continuously shifts between building and degrading molecules to match demand and resource availability.', analogy: 'It is like a city balancing municipal supply with maintenance and construction.' }
163:   ],
164:   membranes: [
165:     { topic: 'the lipid bilayer', correct: 'It is a two-layer membrane arranged with hydrophobic tails inward and hydrophilic heads outward.', wrongs: ['It is made only of amino acids.', 'It is a rigid solid wall with no motion.', 'It has identical heads and tails facing both ways.'], why: 'Amphipathic lipids self-assemble so that polar heads contact water and nonpolar tails avoid it.', analogy: 'It is like a sandwich where the dry parts face inward and the wet parts face outward.' },
166:     { topic: 'the easiest molecule to cross a lipid bilayer', correct: 'A small nonpolar molecule such as oxygen moves across relatively easily.', wrongs: ['A large charged ion crosses freely.', 'A large protein crosses without assistance.', 'A glucose molecule crosses by simple diffusion always.'], why: 'The membrane core is hydrophobic, so small nonpolar species dissolve and diffuse through it best.', analogy: 'It is like a small, nonsticky object slipping through a fence more easily than a bulky charged one.' },
167:     { topic: 'active transport', correct: 'It moves molecules against a gradient and requires energy, usually from ATP or an ion gradient.', wrongs: ['It moves molecules only down the gradient without energy.', 'It requires no proteins.', 'It is always passive diffusion.'], why: 'Active transport works against the natural tendency of molecules to equilibrate, so it must be coupled to an energy source.', analogy: 'It is like carrying water uphill instead of letting it run downhill.' },
168:     { topic: 'osmosis', correct: 'It is the net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane toward higher effective solute concentration.', wrongs: ['It is movement of any solute through any barrier.', 'It only refers to proteins crossing a membrane.', 'It is equal to diffusion of ATP.'], why: 'Water moves to dilute the side with greater osmotic pressure and reduce the chemical potential difference.', analogy: 'It is like water seeking a more crowded side to equalize pressure.' },
169:     { topic: 'the fluid mosaic model', correct: 'It describes a dynamic membrane containing lipids and proteins that move within the bilayer.', wrongs: ['It describes a rigid wall of proteins only.', 'It says every membrane component is fixed permanently.', 'It is only relevant to extracellular matrices.'], why: 'Lateral motion and selective association are key features of membrane architecture.', analogy: 'It is like a flexible collage with parts drifting and rearranging while still staying in place overall.' },
170:     { topic: 'integral membrane proteins', correct: 'They are embedded within the bilayer and often span it with hydrophobic regions.', wrongs: ['They are located only in the cytosol.', 'They never contact the membrane.', 'They are made of only DNA.'], why: 'Hydrophobic segments interact with the lipid core while polar regions face the aqueous phases.', analogy: 'They are like anchors holding a bridge in the middle of a river.' },
171:     { topic: 'peripheral membrane proteins', correct: 'They associate with the membrane surface rather than spanning the bilayer.', wrongs: ['They are always transmembrane helices.', 'They are stored inside the nucleus.', 'They are phospholipids.'], why: 'They often bind via electrostatics or interactions with other membrane proteins or lipids.', analogy: 'They are like workers stationed on the edge of a platform rather than on the main bridge.' },
172:     { topic: 'the role of cholesterol in membranes', correct: 'It modulates membrane fluidity and stability and can reduce permeability to small ions.', wrongs: ['It always makes membranes completely rigid.', 'It removes the need for lipids.', 'It destroys all membrane proteins.'], why: 'Cholesterol intercalates between phospholipids and affects packing and transition temperature.', analogy: 'It is like a shock absorber that tunes a car’s suspension for different road conditions.' },
173:     { topic: 'the effect of unsaturated fatty acids on membranes', correct: 'They increase membrane fluidity by introducing kinks that prevent tight packing.', wrongs: ['They make membranes more rigid by default.', 'They are not part of the membrane at all.', 'They always cause proteins to denature.'], why: 'Double bonds in acyl chains disrupt regular packing and lower the temperature needed for fluidity.', analogy: 'It is like uneven bricks preventing a wall from becoming a perfectly rigid block.' },
174:     { topic: 'facilitated diffusion', correct: 'It allows polar or charged solutes to cross membranes down their gradient through transporters or channels.', wrongs: ['It moves molecules against the gradient without energy.', 'It requires no proteins.', 'It is only used for oxygen.'], why: 'Proteins provide a pathway that avoids the hydrophobic barrier of the membrane.', analogy: 'It is like a gate allowing passengers through a wall without opening the whole barrier.' },
175:     { topic: 'the voltage gradient across a membrane', correct: 'It is an electrical potential difference created by unequal ion distribution across the membrane.', wrongs: ['It is only a pH measure.', 'It is the same as membrane thickness.', 'It is absent in all cells.'], why: 'Ion gradients create charges separated by the membrane, establishing membrane potential.', analogy: 'It is like a battery with opposite charges stored on two sides of a barrier.' },
176:     { topic: 'membrane potential', correct: 'It is the difference in electrical charge across the membrane that can power transport and signaling.', wrongs: ['It is always zero in living cells.', 'It is only relevant in lipids.', 'It is the same as osmotic pressure.'], why: 'Potential energy stored in electrochemical gradients supports many cellular processes.', analogy: 'It is like a charge imbalance stored in a capacitor.' },
177:     { topic: 'ion channels', correct: 'They form pores that allow specific ions to move across membranes down electrochemical gradients.', wrongs: ['They carry only glucose across membranes.', 'They are never selective.', 'They create new ATP in the membrane.'], why: 'Channels permit rapid, highly selective ion movement needed for signaling and transport.', analogy: 'They are like specialized doors for one type of traffic only.' },
178:     { topic: 'transporters versus channels', correct: 'Transporters undergo conformational changes and may be passive or active, while channels usually provide a continuous pore.', wrongs: ['They are identical in every way.', 'Transporters never bind ligands.', 'Channels always require ATP.'], why: 'The structural mechanism differs, affecting kinetics and energy coupling.', analogy: 'It is like a revolving turnstile versus a simple open gate.' },
179:     { topic: 'the importance of membrane asymmetry', correct: 'Different lipids and proteins are distributed differently on the two leaflets, which is important for signaling and function.', wrongs: ['Membranes are perfectly symmetrical everywhere.', 'Asymmetry never matters in cells.', 'Symmetry is always more efficient than asymmetry.'], why: 'The two leaflets often carry different compositions and roles in trafficking and cell signaling.', analogy: 'It is like a building with different functions on each side of a hallway.' },
180:     { topic: 'phospholipid head groups', correct: 'They are hydrophilic and interact with water, while the tails are hydrophobic and avoid it.', wrongs: ['Both ends are identically hydrophobic.', 'Only the tails interact with water.', 'They are always proteins.'], why: 'The head group structure determines polarity and interactions with the environment.', analogy: 'It is like the umbrella handle and canvas that respond differently to rain.' },
181:     { topic: 'the role of membrane proteins in signaling', correct: 'They can detect extracellular signals and transmit information into the cell.', wrongs: ['They never interact with ligands.', 'They only generate ATP.', 'They are only structural and never dynamic.'], why: 'Receptor proteins bind ligands and initiate signal-transduction cascades.', analogy: 'They are like sensors that pass information through a wall.' },
182:     { topic: 'the significance of selective permeability', correct: 'It allows cells to control the movement of solutes and maintain internal conditions.', wrongs: ['It means every molecule crosses equally.', 'It eliminates all gradients.', 'It is only relevant to plant cells.'], why: 'Molecular identity and membrane components determine what can cross and how rapidly.', analogy: 'It is like a customs checkpoint that allows some goods through and holds others back.' },
183:     { topic: 'the effect of membrane rupture', correct: 'It destroys the barrier function and can leak ions and metabolites, disrupting cell homeostasis.', wrongs: ['It always enhances ATP synthesis.', 'It makes the cell stronger.', 'It only affects plant cells.'], why: 'The membrane is essential for establishing gradients and compartmentalization.', analogy: 'It is like breaking the wall of a dam and losing the stored water.' },
184:     { topic: 'why cells need membrane transport proteins', correct: 'Because the lipid bilayer is a poor barrier for most ions and polar molecules.', wrongs: ['Because all molecules dissolve spontaneously in the membrane.', 'Because proteins are not needed in transport.', 'Because ATP is always available without channels.'], why: 'Large or charged molecules cannot pass efficiently through the hydrophobic core without assistance.', analogy: 'It is like needing a ramp instead of a cliff to move a heavy object.' },
185:     { topic: 'simple diffusion', correct: 'It is the net movement of molecules down a concentration gradient without a transporter.', wrongs: ['It requires ATP always.', 'It can move molecules uphill without energy.', 'It is only for proteins.'], why: 'Random molecular motion plus the gradient drives net flux toward equilibrium.', analogy: 'It is like people spreading out from a crowded room without outside help.' },
186:     { topic: 'the role of membrane lipids in signaling', correct: 'Some lipids act as signaling molecules or precursors for second messengers.', wrongs: ['Lipids cannot transmit signals.', 'Only proteins function in signaling.', 'Lipid signaling never involves enzymes.'], why: 'Lipids can be cleaved or modified to create signals that regulate cell behavior.', analogy: 'They are like the notes passed around a system to coordinate actions.' },
187:     { topic: 'the effect of a hypotonic solution on a cell', correct: 'Water enters the cell, potentially causing swelling or lysis if excessive.', wrongs: ['The cell loses water and shrivels.', 'The membrane becomes completely impermeable.', 'The pH drops immediately.'], why: 'The external solute concentration is lower, so water moves into the cell by osmosis.', analogy: 'It is like a sponge taking in water when the surrounding environment is drier.' },
188:     { topic: 'an electrochemical gradient', correct: 'It combines both chemical concentration differences and electrical potential across the membrane.', wrongs: ['It is only the concentration difference.', 'It is only the voltage difference.', 'It is the same as a pH buffer.'], why: 'The total driving force on an ion depends on both its gradient and the membrane potential.', analogy: 'It is like combining both distance and slope to judge how hard a ball will roll.' },
189:     { topic: 'why membranes are described as fluid', correct: 'Because lipids and many proteins move laterally within the membrane plane.', wrongs: ['Because they are completely rigid.', 'Because they never change shape.', 'Because they are always identical in composition.'], why: 'Thermal motion and the weak forces holding membrane components together allow movement.', analogy: 'It is like a fluid surface where people can shift positions without leaving the room.' },
190:     { topic: 'the role of membrane proteins in transport', correct: 'They provide specificity and regulation that permit selective movement of molecules across the barrier.', wrongs: ['They always increase the permeability of all molecules equally.', 'They create ATP from glucose directly.', 'They remove the need for gradients.'], why: 'Transport proteins can recognize certain molecules and couple movement to energy or gradients.', analogy: 'It is like a customs officer checking passports rather than opening all gates.' },
191:     { topic: 'the relevance of membrane curvature', correct: 'It helps shape organelles and supports vesicle formation and trafficking.', wrongs: ['It has no biological meaning.', 'It is only a feature of rigid walls.', 'It permanently blocks all transport.'], why: 'Curvature is generated by lipids, proteins, and cytoskeletal interactions and is essential for vesicle budding.', analogy: 'It is like bending a sheet of paper to create a container from a flat surface.' },
192:     { topic: 'the role of lipid rafts', correct: 'They are membrane microdomains enriched in certain lipids and proteins that can organize signaling.', wrongs: ['They are empty spaces with no function.', 'They are the same as the entire membrane.', 'They are only found in DNA.'], why: 'Lipid packing and protein associations can create localized environments for signaling and trafficking.', analogy: 'It is like a section of a city designed for a specialized purpose.' },
193:     { topic: 'the permeability of a membrane to glucose', correct: 'It is limited because glucose is polar and large, so specific transporters are usually needed.', wrongs: ['It crosses freely because all molecules move through membranes.', 'It is fully nonpolar and should move easily.', 'It is always transported by ATP synthase.'], why: 'The hydrophobic membrane interior does not favor polar molecules, so transporters help them cross.', analogy: 'It is like asking a large, heavy box to navigate a narrow gate without a cart.' },
194:     { topic: 'the effect of membrane composition on temperature tolerance', correct: 'More unsaturated fatty acids generally increase fluidity at lower temperatures, while saturated lipids increase packing.', wrongs: ['Composition never matters for membrane behavior.', 'Only proteins change membrane properties.', 'Lower temperature always makes all membranes more fluid.'], why: 'The arrangement of acyl chains changes the physical state of the membrane.', analogy: 'It is like choosing a different balance of materials to keep a floor stable in summer and winter.' },
195:     { topic: 'the relationship between membranes and organelles', correct: 'They compartmentalize cellular processes by separating distinct biochemical environments within organelles.', wrongs: ['They remove all need for compartments.', 'They are only the outer cell boundary.', 'They only store ATP.'], why: 'Membranes define biological spaces with different compositions and reactions.', analogy: 'It is like separating the kitchen from the dining room to keep jobs organized.' },
196:     { topic: 'the purpose of membrane receptors', correct: 'They bind extracellular signals and trigger intracellular changes that modify cell behavior.', wrongs: ['They only transport ions with no signaling.', 'They are only structural scaffold components.', 'They serve as storage for lipids.'], why: 'The receptor-ligand interaction transduces information across the membrane.', analogy: 'It is like a doorman receiving a message and relaying it to the rest of the building.' },
197:     { topic: 'the effect of water movement on membrane integrity', correct: 'Osmotic changes can change cell volume and membrane tension, influencing function and survival.', wrongs: ['Water never affects membranes because membranes are immobile.', 'Only pH influences membrane integrity.', 'Volume changes do not affect tension.'], why: 'Membranes must accommodate changes in internal pressure and solute balance.', analogy: 'It is like a balloon whose shape changes when the surrounding pressure shifts.' },
198:     { topic: 'the role of phospholipid asymmetry in apoptosis', correct: 'It can expose phosphatidylserine on the outer leaflet and help signal cell death to phagocytes.', wrongs: ['Asymmetry never affects cell behavior.', 'It only affects DNA synthesis.', 'It only matters for bacterial membranes.'], why: 'Membrane composition changes serve as recognition signals in cell physiology.', analogy: 'It is like a flag turning outward to signal a need for help.' }
199:   ],
200:   genetics: [
201:     { topic: 'DNA as the genetic material', correct: 'It stores the instructions for building and maintaining an organism in a chemically stable form.', wrongs: ['It is a membrane lipid.', 'It is only an energy carrier.', 'It is irrelevant to inheritance.'], why: 'DNA’s base sequence encodes genes and is passed on through replication.', analogy: 'It is like the master blueprint stored in a safe.' },
202:     { topic: 'transcription', correct: 'It is the synthesis of RNA from a DNA template.', wrongs: ['It is the assembly of amino acids into proteins.', 'It is the direct copy of DNA into protein.', 'It occurs only in membranes.'], why: 'RNA polymerase reads DNA and synthesizes a complementary RNA strand.', analogy: 'It is like copying information from a master document into a working draft.' },
203:     { topic: 'translation', correct: 'It is the synthesis of a polypeptide at the ribosome according to the mRNA sequence.', wrongs: ['It is the synthesis of DNA from RNA.', 'It occurs only in the nucleus.', 'It creates phospholipids.'], why: 'Ribosomes decode codons and link amino acids in the correct order.', analogy: 'It is like a factory using a set of instructions to assemble a chain from parts.' },
204:     { topic: 'a codon', correct: 'It is a three-nucleotide unit in mRNA that specifies an amino acid or a stop signal.', wrongs: ['It is a whole chromosome.', 'It is a lipid molecule.', 'It is a protein polymer.'], why: 'The genetic code is read in triplets during translation.', analogy: 'It is like a three-letter command in a coded instruction set.' },
205:     { topic: 'RNA bases', correct: 'RNA contains adenine, uracil, cytosine, and guanine.', wrongs: ['RNA contains thymine instead of uracil.', 'RNA has no nitrogenous bases.', 'RNA contains only adenine and guanine.'], why: 'Uracil replaces thymine in RNA and pairs with adenine.', analogy: 'It is like a similar toolkit with one different tool for a different job.' },
206:     { topic: 'DNA base pairing', correct: 'Adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine.', wrongs: ['Adenine pairs with cytosine.', 'Guanine pairs with thymine.', 'All bases pair randomly.'], why: 'Complementary hydrogen bonding gives DNA its consistent double-helix structure.', analogy: 'It is like a zipper with matching teeth that fit together only one way.' },
207:     { topic: 'the purpose of the genetic code', correct: 'It defines how nucleotide triplets correspond to amino acids or stop signals.', wrongs: ['It defines membrane lipid composition.', 'It is irrelevant to protein synthesis.', 'It only codes for ATP.'], why: 'The code translates genes into proteins with predictable sequences.', analogy: 'It is like a dictionary linking words to their meanings.' },
208:     { topic: 'the central dogma', correct: 'It describes the flow of information from DNA to RNA to protein.', wrongs: ['It describes only protein folding.', 'It says proteins become DNA directly.', 'It ignores RNA entirely.'], why: 'Information usually moves through transcription and translation in this order.', analogy: 'It is like a chain of communication from a master source to a working copy to a final product.' },
209:     { topic: 'DNA replication', correct: 'It copies the DNA molecule so each daughter cell receives a complete genome.', wrongs: ['It turns DNA into ATP.', 'It converts RNA into proteins immediately.', 'It makes only one strand.'], why: 'Semiconservative replication preserves information through cell division.', analogy: 'It is like photocopying the master plans before handing them to two teams.' },
210:     { topic: 'the role of polymerase', correct: 'It synthesizes nucleic acid chains by adding nucleotides in a template-directed way.', wrongs: ['It directly builds amino acids.', 'It is only used in membranes.', 'It always breaks DNA.'], why: 'DNA and RNA polymerases read a template and add complementary nucleotides.', analogy: 'It is like a machine assembling pieces according to a pattern template.' },
211:     { topic: 'the meaning of a mutation', correct: 'It is a change in DNA sequence that can affect gene product function depending on the location and type of change.', wrongs: ['It is always harmless.', 'It is only a change in RNA.', 'It always creates a new protein from scratch.'], why: 'Mutations can change amino acid sequence, regulation, or expression patterns.', analogy: 'It is like altering one word in a recipe and changing the final dish.' },
212:     { topic: 'the significance of DNA repair', correct: 'It reduces the accumulation of mutations and preserves genome integrity.', wrongs: ['It is unnecessary because cells never damage DNA.', 'It always changes the DNA sequence intentionally.', 'It is only important in the membrane.'], why: 'Cells face chemical and physical damage, so repair systems maintain sequence fidelity.', analogy: 'It is like fixing small errors before they become a larger problem.' },
213:     { topic: 'the role of mRNA', correct: 'It carries the genetic message from DNA to the ribosome for translation.', wrongs: ['It stores the long-term genome.', 'It acts as the main enzyme catalyst.', 'It carries phospholipids.'], why: 'mRNA is the transient intermediate between gene and protein.', analogy: 'It is like the working manual carried to the assembly line.' },
214:     { topic: 'the role of tRNA', correct: 'It brings the correct amino acid to the ribosome by matching its anticodon to the codon in mRNA.', wrongs: ['It stores the entire DNA sequence.', 'It acts as a lipid carrier.', 'It is the main site of transcription.'], why: 'The anticodon-codon interaction ensures the correct amino acid is incorporated.', analogy: 'It is like the courier that brings the matching part to the correct assembly station.' },
215:     { topic: 'ribosomes', correct: 'They are the molecular machines that assemble polypeptides from amino acids during translation.', wrongs: ['They are the sites of DNA replication.', 'They are the ATP energy currency.', 'They synthesize lipids only.'], why: 'Ribosomes catalyze peptide-bond formation while decoding the mRNA message.', analogy: 'They are like the assembly line machinery in a factory.' },
216:     { topic: 'gene expression', correct: 'It is the process by which genetic information is used to produce a functional gene product, often a protein.', wrongs: ['It only refers to DNA replication.', 'It includes only membrane transport.', 'It never involves RNA.'], why: 'Cells regulate when and where genes are turned on, influencing phenotype and function.', analogy: 'It is like deciding which tools to use at different stages of construction.' },
217:     { topic: 'a promoter', correct: 'It is a DNA sequence that helps recruit the transcription machinery to start gene expression.', wrongs: ['It is the amino acid sequence of a protein.', 'It is always the stop codon.', 'It is the membrane protein site.'], why: 'Promoters provide binding sites for transcription factors and RNA polymerase.', analogy: 'It is like the starting flag at a race that marks where the run begins.' },
218:     { topic: 'a terminator sequence', correct: 'It signals RNA polymerase to stop transcription.', wrongs: ['It is a start codon for translation.', 'It is a lipid head group.', 'It defines the gene’s ribosome binding site.'], why: 'Termination ensures transcripts end in the correct place and do not read through neighboring genes.', analogy: 'It is like the stop sign at the end of a road.' },
219:     { topic: 'the genetic code being degenerate', correct: 'It means multiple codons can specify the same amino acid.', wrongs: ['It means every codon encodes a different amino acid.', 'It means RNA contains no genetic information.', 'It means proteins are always identical.'], why: 'Degeneracy protects against some point mutations and allows variation without changing the amino acid sequence.', analogy: 'It is like having several different keys open the same door.' },
220:     { topic: 'the role of histones', correct: 'They are DNA-binding proteins that help package chromosomal DNA and regulate access to genes.', wrongs: ['They are enzymes that synthesize ATP.', 'They are membrane lipids.', 'They are only found in RNA.'], why: 'Histones compact DNA and modulate transcription by controlling chromatin structure.', analogy: 'They are like the packaging and shelving that organize a large collection of materials.' },
221:     { topic: 'epigenetics', correct: 'It involves chemical or structural regulation of gene expression without altering the DNA sequence itself.', wrongs: ['It changes the DNA sequence itself.', 'It is another name for translation.', 'It only affects membrane transport.'], why: 'DNA methylation, histone modifications, and chromatin structure influence when genes are active.', analogy: 'It is like adjusting how loudly a radio plays without changing the station itself.' },
222:     { topic: 'a frameshift mutation', correct: 'It changes the reading frame by insertion or deletion of nucleotides not in multiples of three.', wrongs: ['It always changes only one base pair without effect.', 'It only affects rRNA.', 'It only occurs in proteins.'], why: 'Shifting the codon frame alters all downstream amino acids and often destroys protein function.', analogy: 'It is like removing a letter from a sentence and making every subsequent word misread.' },
223:     { topic: 'a nonsense mutation', correct: 'It creates a premature stop codon and usually truncates the protein.', wrongs: ['It adds extra amino acids to the end of the protein.', 'It makes a protein more stable by definition.', 'It only influences the DNA template.'], why: 'Premature termination prevents the full-length protein from being produced.', analogy: 'It is like a sentence ending early before the important message is finished.' },
224:     { topic: 'the role of RNA splicing', correct: 'It removes introns and joins exons to produce a mature mRNA message in eukaryotes.', wrongs: ['It translates RNA into DNA.', 'It only occurs in prokaryotes.', 'It removes exons from mRNA.'], why: 'Splicing allows one gene to generate multiple protein variants and refine the transcript.', analogy: 'It is like trimming out the unusable parts of a blueprint before building.' },
225:     { topic: 'the function of promoters and enhancers', correct: 'They regulate transcription by attracting or stabilizing the transcriptional machinery and associated factors.', wrongs: ['They are always translated into protein.', 'They are membrane transporters.', 'They are only present in RNA.'], why: 'Gene expression depends on sequence-specific binding of transcription factors to regulatory DNA motifs.', analogy: 'They are like traffic signals and lane markers controlling when and how traffic moves.' },
226:     { topic: 'the significance of the template strand', correct: 'It is the DNA strand read by RNA polymerase to direct synthesis of complementary RNA.', wrongs: ['It is the strand made into protein directly.', 'It is always the coding strand.', 'It contains only uracil.'], why: 'RNA polymerase copies the DNA template into a complementary RNA transcript.', analogy: 'It is like the original pattern used to guide a copy.' },
227:     { topic: 'the purpose of the coding strand', correct: 'It has the same base sequence as the RNA transcript except thymine is replaced by uracil.', wrongs: ['It is never paired with the template strand.', 'It is the strand that is always translated directly.', 'It contains no genetic information.'], why: 'The coding strand matches the RNA sequence, while the template strand is read by polymerase.', analogy: 'It is like the final draft compared to the original pattern used to create it.' },
228:     { topic: 'DNA replication fidelity', correct: 'It relies on accurate base pairing and proofreading to preserve the genetic message.', wrongs: ['It is random and does not need accuracy.', 'It only depends on protein concentration.', 'It always introduces mutations for diversity.'], why: 'The cell invests in high-fidelity copying so daughter cells inherit correct information.', analogy: 'It is like a careful copy machine that checks for mistakes before printing.' },
229:     { topic: 'the role of telomeres', correct: 'They are protective caps at chromosome ends that help prevent loss of essential DNA during replication.', wrongs: ['They are enzymes that degrade DNA.', 'They are the coding regions for proteins.', 'They are only in bacterial cells.'], why: 'Replication of chromosome ends is incomplete, so telomeres buffer against loss of coding sequence.', analogy: 'They are like plastic caps on the ends of shoelaces to keep them from fraying.' },
230:     { topic: 'the role of restriction enzymes', correct: 'They recognize specific DNA sequences and can cut DNA at defined positions.', wrongs: ['They synthesize DNA chains.', 'They translate RNA into protein.', 'They are only used in membrane transport.'], why: 'Restriction enzymes are used in cloning and molecular biology because of their precise sequence specificity.', analogy: 'They are like molecular scissors that cut only where a particular pattern is marked.' },
231:     { topic: 'the role of PCR', correct: 'It amplifies specific DNA sequences through repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing, and extension.', wrongs: ['It directly translates DNA into protein.', 'It always alters the DNA sequence in a random way.', 'It is used only for ATP production.'], why: 'PCR exploits DNA polymerase and temperature cycling to copy a target sequence dramatically.', analogy: 'It is like making many identical copies of one page in a print run.' },
232:     { topic: 'the meaning of a genome', correct: 'It is the complete collection of genetic information in an organism or cell.', wrongs: ['It is only the RNA content.', 'It is the set of all membranes in a cell.', 'It is the entire collection of proteins.'], why: 'The genome includes all chromosomes and genes required for development and function.', analogy: 'It is like the complete instruction library for a whole building.' },
233:     { topic: 'the relationship between genotype and phenotype', correct: 'Genotype is the DNA sequence, while phenotype is the observable trait or functional consequence.', wrongs: ['Phenotype is the DNA sequence itself.', 'Genotype is always visible without measuring anything.', 'They are identical in every organism.'], why: 'Genes influence proteins and development, which together produce observable traits.', analogy: 'It is like the recipe versus the dish that comes out of the kitchen.' },
234:     { topic: 'the purpose of DNA methylation', correct: 'It can repress or regulate gene expression by altering DNA accessibility and recruitment of factors.', wrongs: ['It directly creates ATP.', 'It changes an amino acid sequence of the protein.', 'It only acts in the cytoplasm without effect on the nucleus.'], why: 'Chemical marks on DNA influence transcriptional regulation and developmental programs.', analogy: 'It is like adding a label that says “quiet this section” on a document.' },
235:     { topic: 'the role of anticodons', correct: 'They are sequences in tRNA that base-pair with complementary codons in mRNA.', wrongs: ['They are produced by ribosomes to make proteins.', 'They are the same as amino acids.', 'They bind to phospholipids.'], why: 'Anticodon pairing ensures the correct amino acid is delivered during translation.', analogy: 'It is like a key matching a lock with the exact right shape.' },

## Objective
- Complete the existing biochemistry quiz game as a playable game based on Lehninger’s *Principles of Biochemistry*, sixth edition.
- Preserve wrong-answer explanations and add feedback that reviews and corrects players’ written analogies.

## Requirements
- Add more chapters, aiming for 40 questions per chapter.
- Offer only 5 questions per quiz.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking clarifying questions; briefly note them upon completion.

## Decisions
- Use original questions broadly aligned with the textbook’s themes rather than reproducing textbook wording.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected `game.js`, `bank-a.js`, `index.html`, and `styles.css` for the existing game structure and integration points.

### Active
- Integrate the question bank with the existing game and expand chapter question coverage.
- Limit each quiz to five questions.
- Implement analogy review and correction while preserving wrong-answer explanations.
- Run and verify the game.

### Blocked
- An earlier background question-bank authoring task ended with `Fusion request unavailable`; its placeholder file was replaced with the current `bank-a.js`.

## Next Move
1. Inspect the complete contents of `game.js` and `bank-a.js`, including chapter metadata and question counts.
2. Connect the bank to quiz generation, implement five-question quizzes, and add analogy feedback/correction.
3. Run and verify the game; briefly report reasonable assumptions.

## Relevant Files
- `game.js`: Existing chapters, rendering, answer flow, analogy UI, and quiz logic.
- `bank-a.js`: Untracked original biochemistry question data for six chapters.
- `index.html`: Game interface and script loading order.
- `styles.css`: Existing styles for the game and any new feedback UI.

## Important Context
- The user owns a copy of Lehninger’s *Principles of Biochemistry*, sixth edition.
- Changes are uncommitted; `bank-a.js` is reported as untracked. No runtime or browser verification has been completed.

3:     { q: 'What kind of bond links amino acids together in a protein?', answers: [
4:       ['A peptide bond', true, 'A peptide bond forms between the amino group of one amino acid and the carboxyl group of another, joining them into a chain. Think of it as the sturdy link in a molecular necklace.'],
5:       ['A hydrogen bond', false, 'Hydrogen bonds help stabilize protein shapes, but they do not join amino acids into the chain itself. The chain is held together by peptide bonds.'],
6:       ['An ionic bond', false, 'Ionic attractions can help a protein fold, but they are not the repeating links in its backbone. Amino acids are connected by peptide bonds.'],
7:       ['A phosphodiester bond', false, 'Phosphodiester bonds connect nucleotides in DNA and RNA. Amino acids in proteins are joined by peptide bonds.']] },
8:     { q: 'Which part of an amino acid varies from one amino acid to another?', answers: [
9:       ['The R group (side chain)', true, 'The R group is the variable side chain. Its chemistry—size, charge, polarity—gives each amino acid its personality and helps determine how proteins fold.'],
10:       ['The amino group', false, 'The amino group is shared by the standard amino acids. It is the side chain, or R group, that changes and makes each one distinct.'],
11:       ['The alpha carbon', false, 'The alpha carbon is the central carbon shared by standard amino acids. The attached R group is the part that varies.'],
12:       ['The carboxyl group', false, 'The carboxyl group is common to amino acids. Look to the R group for the feature that differs from one amino acid to another.']] },
13:     { q: 'A molecule with many polar bonds is most likely to dissolve in…', answers: [

15:       ['Oil', false, 'Oil is mostly nonpolar, so it tends to mix with other nonpolar substances rather than polar molecules. Water is the better match for a polar solute.'],
16:       ['A fatty acid tail', false, 'Fatty acid tails are hydrophobic and nonpolar. A polar molecule is more at home in water than among these tails.'],
17:       ['A vacuum', false, 'A vacuum contains no solvent to dissolve anything. Polar molecules are generally soluble in a polar solvent such as water.']] },
18:     { q: 'What does a buffer do when a small amount of acid is added?', answers: [

20:       ['It makes the solution instantly neutral', false, 'Buffers do not automatically force pH to 7. They resist changes, keeping pH in a useful range.'],
21:       ['It releases only hydroxide ions', false, 'A buffer is a paired system that can take up or donate protons depending on what is added. It does not simply release hydroxide.'],
22:       ['It permanently removes all acid', false, 'A buffer can bind some of the added H⁺, but its capacity is limited. Enough acid will overwhelm it.']] },

25:       ['Iron', false, 'Iron is essential in some proteins, but it is not present in every organic molecule. Carbon is the defining element of organic chemistry.'],
26:       ['Sodium', false, 'Sodium is an important ion in cells, but it is not universal in organic molecules. Carbon is the common backbone element.'],
27:       ['Phosphorus', false, 'Phosphorus appears in molecules such as ATP and nucleic acids, but many organic molecules contain none. Carbon is the universal feature.']] }

31:       ['Hydrogen bonds between molecules', true, 'Water is polar: oxygen pulls electrons more strongly than hydrogen. Neighboring molecules attract through hydrogen bonds, giving water its cohesion.'],
32:       ['Peptide bonds between molecules', false, 'Peptide bonds link amino acids in proteins. Water molecules attract each other mainly through hydrogen bonds.'],
33:       ['They share electrons permanently', false, 'Water’s O–H bonds are polar covalent, but neighboring water molecules do not share electrons with each other. They form hydrogen bonds.'],
34:       ['Water molecules are nonpolar', false, 'Water is decidedly polar. Its bent shape and unequal charge distribution allow hydrogen bonds between molecules.']] },
35:     { q: 'A solution at pH 3 is how many times more acidic than one at pH 5?', answers: [
36:       ['100 times', true, 'The pH scale is logarithmic. A two-unit drop means 10², or 100 times, more hydrogen ion concentration.'],
37:       ['2 times', false, 'Each pH unit is a tenfold change, not a onefold step. Two pH units mean 10 × 10 = 100 times.'],
38:       ['10 times', false, 'A one-unit difference is tenfold. From pH 5 to pH 3 is two units, so the difference is 100-fold.'],
39:       ['1,000 times', false, 'A three-unit difference would be 1,000-fold. Here the difference is two units: 100-fold.']] },
40:     { q: 'Which water property helps sweat cool your skin as it evaporates?', answers: [
41:       ['High heat of vaporization', true, 'Evaporating water takes substantial energy to break intermolecular attractions. It pulls that heat from your skin, cooling it.'],
42:       ['Low surface tension', false, 'Surface tension explains the “skin” at water’s surface, not the cooling effect of evaporation. Cooling comes from water’s high heat of vaporization.'],
43:       ['Its ability to freeze at room temperature', false, 'Water freezes below its normal freezing point, not at room temperature. Evaporation cools you because it requires significant heat energy.'],
44:       ['Its nonpolar nature', false, 'Water is polar. Its strong attractions take energy to overcome during evaporation, which is why sweat can cool you.']] },
45:     { q: 'In water, a hydrophobic molecule tends to…', answers: [
46:       ['Cluster away from water', true, 'Hydrophobic molecules are usually nonpolar. They do not make favorable interactions with water, so they gather together and minimize contact with it.'],
47:       ['Form hydrogen bonds with water', false, 'Hydrophobic molecules generally lack the charged or polar groups needed for favorable hydrogen bonds with water.'],
48:       ['Dissolve better than salt', false, 'Salt dissolves readily because water stabilizes its ions. Hydrophobic molecules generally do not dissolve well in water.'],
49:       ['Split water into oxygen and hydrogen', false, 'Hydrophobicity describes poor mixing with water, not a reaction that breaks water apart. Hydrophobic molecules tend to cluster together.']] },
50:     { q: 'What is the conjugate base of carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) after it loses one proton?', answers: [
51:       ['Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)', true, 'Losing one H⁺ from H₂CO₃ leaves HCO₃⁻, bicarbonate. This pair is part of an important blood-buffer system.'],
52:       ['Carbonate (CO₃²⁻)', false, 'Carbonate forms after carbonic acid loses two protons. Losing one proton gives bicarbonate, HCO₃⁻.'],
53:       ['Carbon dioxide (CO₂)', false, 'CO₂ can react with water to form carbonic acid, but it is not the conjugate base formed by losing one proton.'],
54:       ['Hydroxide (OH⁻)', false, 'Hydroxide is a separate base. When carbonic acid loses one proton, its conjugate base is bicarbonate.']] }
55:   ]},

64:       ['Making the products more energetic', false, 'An enzyme changes the rate by lowering the activation barrier; it does not raise product energy or alter the reaction’s overall energy balance.'],

69:       ['It becomes a DNA-binding site', false, 'Denaturation disrupts protein structure; it does not transform an active site into a new type of site.'],

79:       ['It destroys every enzyme in the cell', false, 'Competitive inhibition is reversible binding in the classic model, not wholesale enzyme destruction. The inhibitor competes for the active site.'],

81:       ['It permanently changes the DNA sequence', false, 'Inhibitors act on enzyme molecules, not by rewriting DNA. A competitive inhibitor competes at the active site.']] }

- Add more chapters, aiming for 40 questions per chapter.
- Offer only 5 questions per quiz.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking clarifying questions; briefly note them upon completion.
